sections.0.body.0.t: An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is the equivalent of a food's nutrition label: a structured document listing all the components that make up a software artifact: direct and transitive dependencies, exact versions, licenses and cryptographic hashes.

sections.1.body.0.t: The two dominant standards are CycloneDX and SPDX. A real excerpt from a CycloneDX SBOM, reduced to a single component:

sections.2.body.0.t: The purl (package URL) is the component's universal identifier: pkg:npm/lodash@4.17.15 states the ecosystem, the name and the exact version, in a format any system can query. The hashes prove the component is exactly what the SBOM says it is, leaving no room for a silent swap.

sections.2.body.1.t: In practice, the SBOM is generated in the pipeline's package stage, by SCA tools or dedicated generators like Syft, and published (ideally signed) alongside the artifact.

sections.3.body.0.t: When the next critical vulnerability breaks in a popular library, the question is always the same: are we affected? With an SBOM, the answer comes in minutes: a search for the purl across the inventory of all services. Without one, it takes days digging project by project, or worse: finding out in production.

sections.3.body.1.t: It has also become a market requirement: US government agencies began requiring SBOMs from software vendors, and enterprise customers are following the same path.

sections.3.heading.t: Why it matters: the next Log4Shell test

sections.4.body.0.t: SCA and SBOM feed each other: composition analysis produces the inventory, and the inventory is what allows continuously monitoring the components against new CVEs. An SBOM generated once and forgotten ages fast: the value is in the living cycle: generate on every build, monitor always.

tagline.t: A formal inventory of everything that makes up the artifact: dependencies, versions, licenses and hashes.
